items.prompt_md: In the monotonic-deque solution for window maximum, what does the deque hold and how is it ordered?
options: Values of the window in sorted ascending order
Indices of elements, ordered so the values decrease from front to back
Indices in increasing order, with values increasing too
Only the current maximum and the current minimum
items.answer: Indices of elements, ordered so the values decrease from front to back
items.explanation_md: The deque stores indices so that you can tell when the front has left the window, and their values decrease front to back so the front is the max. An ascending order would put the minimum in front, and keeping just two values loses the runner-ups you need after the max expires.

items.prompt_md: Why is it safe to pop every back element that is `<=` the newcomer?
options: Those elements are older and not larger, so they leave the window first and can never be the maximum while the newcomer is present
They are smaller, so they are not needed for any later window regardless of position
Popping keeps the deque sorted ascending for binary search
They are duplicates and the problem forbids equal values
items.answer: Those elements are older and not larger, so they leave the window first and can never be the maximum while the newcomer is present
items.explanation_md: Older means it expires earlier; not larger means it never wins while the newcomer is alive. 'Smaller' alone is not the reason: a smaller element that is *newer* must be kept, because it may outlive the bigger one.

items.prompt_md: With window size `k`, at step `i` when should the front index be removed?
options: When the front index is `< i - k - 1`
When the front index equals `k`
Whenever a new element is larger than the front value
When the front index is `<= i - k`, because the window covers `i - k + 1 .. i`
items.answer: When the front index is `<= i - k`, because the window covers `i - k + 1 .. i`
items.explanation_md: The window holds the last `k` indices, so anything at or below `i - k` is outside. Comparing against `k` itself mixes up positions and window length; and a larger newcomer removes from the *back* in the other loop, not from the front.

items.prompt_md: Why does the deque store indices rather than values?
options: Indices take less memory than integers
Values would make the deque unsortable
You must know the position of the front to tell when it has slid out of the window; the value can be read back via `nums[index]`
Indices let you binary search for the maximum
items.answer: You must know the position of the front to tell when it has slid out of the window; the value can be read back via `nums[index]`
items.explanation_md: Expiry is a positional question, and a value cannot answer it (equal values may appear many times). Memory size and binary search are not the reason; the front is always the max anyway.

items.prompt_md: What is the total time to compute all window maxima for an array of length `n` using the deque?
options: O(n log k), because each push may bubble through the deque
O(n), because each index is pushed once and popped at most once overall
O(n * k), because each step rescans the deque
O(k), because only the last window matters
items.answer: O(n), because each index is pushed once and popped at most once overall
items.explanation_md: The inner `while` looks quadratic but the total number of pops can never exceed the number of pushes, which is `n`. O(n log k) is the heap's cost, and O(n*k) is the brute force.

items.prompt_md: How much extra space does the deque solution use besides the output list?
options: O(k), since expired indices are removed and at most `k` indices are inside the window
O(1), since a deque is a constant-size structure
O(n), since every index is kept until the end
O(log k), because the deque is balanced like a heap
items.answer: O(k), since expired indices are removed and at most `k` indices are inside the window
items.explanation_md: At most `k` indices can be inside the window at once, and expired ones are popped from the front. A deque is not constant-size: for a strictly decreasing array it fills to `k`.

items.prompt_md: A max-heap with lazy deletion also solves window maximum. What is its time complexity compared with the deque?
options: O(n), the same as the deque
O(n * k), because it has to rebuild the heap per window
O(log n) total, since the heap is always sorted
O(n log n) worst case with lazy deletion (or O(n log k) if cleaned), versus O(n) for the deque
items.answer: O(n log n) worst case with lazy deletion (or O(n log k) if cleaned), versus O(n) for the deque
items.explanation_md: Every heap push/pop costs a logarithm and stale entries only get discarded when they surface. The deque avoids the log because it exploits the age ordering that a heap ignores.

items.prompt_md: Trace `nums = [5, 1, 4, 2]` with `k = 2`. After processing `i = 2` (and doing the expiry check), what indices does the deque hold?
options: `[0, 2]`: the `5` still stays because it is the largest
`[1, 2]`: the `1` is kept behind the `4`
`[2]`: the `1` is popped by `4`, then the `5` at index 0 expires since `0 <= 2 - 2`
`[0, 1, 2]`: nothing is popped since the values are not sorted
items.answer: `[2]`: the `1` is popped by `4`, then the `5` at index 0 expires since `0 <= 2 - 2`
items.explanation_md: Before `i = 2` the deque is `[0, 1]`. The `4` pops index 1 (`1 <= 4`) but not index 0 (`5 > 4`). Then the expiry check fires: `0 <= 2 - 2`. The `5` is outside the window `[1, 4]`, so the deque is `[2]` and the answer for this window is `4`.

items.prompt_md: The input is strictly decreasing, like `[9, 7, 5, 3, 1]`. What happens to the deque with window size 3?
options: The deque is cleared at every step
Nothing is popped from the back; each step only the front expires, so the deque stays at size 3
The deque always holds only one index
The deque grows to size `n` because nothing expires
items.answer: Nothing is popped from the back; each step only the front expires, so the deque stays at size 3
items.explanation_md: A decreasing array already satisfies the invariant, so nothing is popped from the back. Old fronts expire from the front, capping the size at `k`. This is the worst case for space, not for time.

items.prompt_md: Why can't a plain monotonic **stack** (as in the next-greater-element pattern) solve window maximum directly?
options: A stack only removes from one end, but window elements must also expire from the oldest end, which needs a deque
A stack cannot hold indices
A stack is limited to O(log n) elements
A stack always keeps values in ascending order
items.answer: A stack only removes from one end, but window elements must also expire from the oldest end, which needs a deque
items.explanation_md: The stack ordering idea is the same, but its elements never expire by position. The window slides, so the oldest element has to be removed from the opposite end.

items.prompt_md: What happens if you pop from the back only while the back value is strictly `<` the newcomer (instead of `<=`)?
options: The answers become wrong whenever two equal maxima appear
The algorithm becomes O(n^2)
The front is no longer the window maximum
The answers stay correct; the deque merely keeps equal values (non-increasing), and the time stays O(n)
items.answer: The answers stay correct; the deque merely keeps equal values (non-increasing), and the time stays O(n)
items.explanation_md: Equal values are harmless: the front is still a maximum, and each index is still pushed and popped once. Using `<=` just keeps the deque tidier and slightly smaller.

items.prompt_md: A monitoring tool receives millions of request latencies in order. After every request, it must report the worst latency among the most recent 500 requests, in total linear time.
options: Max-heap, popping the top each step
Monotonic stack of previous greater values
Sliding window with a monotonic deque of indices
Prefix sums of the latencies
items.answer: Sliding window with a monotonic deque of indices
items.explanation_md: 'Worst of the last k, after every step' is the window-maximum fingerprint. A heap works but costs a log factor and needs lazy deletion; a stack never expires old items; prefix sums answer sums, not maxima.

items.prompt_md: Given daily readings, find the longest stretch of consecutive days in which the highest and lowest readings differ by at most a given tolerance.
options: Sort the readings and take the longest run
A variable-size window that tracks its max and min with two monotonic deques
A fixed-size window with a running sum
Binary search on the stretch length with a hash set
items.answer: A variable-size window that tracks its max and min with two monotonic deques
items.explanation_md: The window grows and shrinks on a condition (spread within tolerance), and checking the condition needs the window max and min in O(1) amortised, which two monotonic deques give. Sorting destroys contiguity; a running sum cannot tell you the spread.

items.prompt_md: A game board has a score on each square. You start on square 0, each move goes forward by 1 to `m` squares, and you collect the score on every square you land on. You want the best total on reaching the last square, and `n` is 100,000.
options: DP where each state needs the best of the previous `m` states, kept in a monotonic deque
Greedy: always jump to the highest-score square in range
Plain recursion without memoisation
Binary search on the final total
items.answer: DP where each state needs the best of the previous `m` states, kept in a monotonic deque
items.explanation_md: dp[i] = score[i] + max(dp[i-m .. i-1]) is a window maximum at every step. The deque makes it O(n). Greedy jumping to the best next square can walk into a bad region; plain recursion is exponential.

items.prompt_md: For every position in a long list of sensor values, report the smallest value among the next 4 positions, in one pass and O(1) work per position.
options: Sort each group of 4 values
Two pointers moving inward from both ends
A trie keyed on the digits of each value
Sliding window with a monotonic deque of indices (tracking the minimum)
items.answer: Sliding window with a monotonic deque of indices (tracking the minimum)
items.explanation_md: The window is fixed-size and the aggregate is a minimum, so the same deque works with the comparison flipped. Sorting every group of four costs a factor more and two pointers do not apply.

items.prompt_md: A trading app tracks a stream of prices and always wants the lowest price in the last 60 ticks, appended one tick at a time, with a hard O(1) amortised update per tick.
options: A min-heap with lazy deletion
Binary search over a sorted copy
Monotonic deque of indices with prices increasing front to back
A hash map from price to count
items.answer: Monotonic deque of indices with prices increasing front to back
items.explanation_md: O(1) amortised per tick rules out a heap's logarithm. The deque keeps only candidates that can still become the minimum and expires the oldest from the front.

items.prompt_md: For each day in a list of daily temperatures, find how many days you must wait until a warmer one (or 0 if none), with no window size involved.
options: Sliding window with a monotonic deque of indices
Monotonic stack of pending days
Sorting the temperatures
Fixed-size window with a running sum
items.answer: Monotonic stack of pending days
items.explanation_md: 'Next greater element to the right' has no expiry by position, so one open end is enough: a monotonic stack. The deque would work but adds an unused second end.

items.prompt_md: Report the sum of every block of 7 consecutive days in a sales log, then identify the best week.
options: Fixed-size window with a running sum (add the new day, subtract the day that left)
Sliding window with a monotonic deque of indices
Max-heap of the daily values
Monotonic stack
items.answer: Fixed-size window with a running sum (add the new day, subtract the day that left)
items.explanation_md: A sum has an inverse, so adding the entering value and subtracting the leaving one suffices. A deque is for maximum/minimum, which have no inverse.

items.prompt_md: From an unsorted array, you need the 5th largest value once.
options: Sliding window with a monotonic deque of indices
Two pointers on the sorted array
Prefix sums
A size-5 min-heap, or a selection algorithm
items.answer: A size-5 min-heap, or a selection algorithm
items.explanation_md: There is no sliding window here; you want an order statistic of the whole array. A small heap handles it in O(n log 5). The deque only answers questions about contiguous windows.

items.prompt_md: Given a sorted array and a target, check whether any two values add up to it.
options: Sliding window with a monotonic deque of indices
A max-heap of the values
Two pointers moving inward from both ends
A monotonic stack
items.answer: Two pointers moving inward from both ends
items.explanation_md: Sortedness lets you discard one end each step. There is no window sliding across positions, so the deque is irrelevant.

items.prompt_md: Find the longest substring that contains no repeated character.
options: Sliding window with a monotonic deque of indices
A variable-size window with a hash map/set of what is inside
A monotonic stack of letters
A max-heap of last-seen positions
items.answer: A variable-size window with a hash map/set of what is inside
items.explanation_md: The condition is about duplicates, not about a maximum or minimum of the window, so a window with a set/map is enough. The deque adds nothing.

items.prompt_md: Count the contiguous subarrays of a list of integers (negatives allowed) whose sum equals exactly a target.
options: Prefix sums with a hash map of how many times each prefix has occurred
Sliding window with a monotonic deque of indices
A variable-size window that shrinks when the sum is too big
A min-heap of prefix sums
items.answer: Prefix sums with a hash map of how many times each prefix has occurred
items.explanation_md: Negatives break the monotonic behaviour a shrinking window relies on. Counting pairs of equal-difference prefixes with a hash map is the correct tool.
